subject: Questions About Large Differences Between DIC and WAIC

messages.author: 1d0b9cb7b66f451c
messages.subject: Questions About Large Differences Between DIC and WAIC
parts:
Hello everyone,


I am a new user on the forum and I am just starting to use INLA. I am working on spatiotemporal models and I have a question that I hope you can help me solve.


I am currently fitting spatiotemporal models with interaction random effects following the Knorr-Held scheme, that is, using the Kronecker product to combine the spatial and temporal effect structure matrices (types I, II, III or IV). My idea is to fit models with various structures for both interaction effects and direct effects of time (iid, RW1, RW2) and space (LCAR, ICAR, etc.), comparing them using fit measures such as DIC and WAIC, and also using predictive measures such as CPO.


When comparing the models, I expected to find close values ​​between DIC and WAIC, since both are based on model likelihood, with slight differences arising from their definitions. However, I have been surprised to find very large differences in several models, on the order of 10^3. This makes model selection difficult and makes me wonder if I am making a mistake in the model specification or violating one of its assumptions.


On the forum I found a comment that said:

"However, sometimes you get a massive difference in DIC or WAIC, like 10000. That gives you a strong hint that one of the models are better."

However, I would like to understand more in depth why these differences occur and how to interpret them.


To give more context, I'm sharing an example of the code I'm using to fit the models in INLA:


sdunif = "expression:

logdens=-log_precision/2;

return(logdens)"


lunif = "expression:

a = 1;

b = 1;

beta = exp(theta)/(1+exp(theta));

logdens = lgamma(a+b)-lgamma(a)-lgamma(b)+(a-1)*log(beta)+(b-1)*log(1-beta);

log_jacobian = log(beta*(1-beta));

return(logdens+log_jacobian)"


g <- inla.read.graph("...")


Qs <- matrix(0, g$n, g$n)

for (i in 1:g$n) {

Qs[i, i] = g$nnbs[[i]]

Qs[i, g$nbs[[i]]] = -1

}

R.Leroux <- diag(dim(Qs)[1]) - Qs


mod.st0 <- inla(O ~ f(ID_muni, model = "generic1", Cmatrix = R.Leroux, constr = TRUE,

hyper = list(prec = list(prior = sdunif), beta = list(prior = lunif, initial = 0))) +

f(ID_year, model = "iid", constr = TRUE,

hyper = list(prec = list(prior = "pc.prec", param = c(1, 0.01)))),

family = "poisson", data = Data_sp, E = E,

control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE, cdf = c(log(1))),

control.fixed = list(mean.intercept = 0, prec.intercept = 0.001),

control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, waic = TRUE, cpo = TRUE),

control.inla = list(strategy = "simplified.laplace"),

num.threads = 4)


Results obtained for this model:


Specifically, with this model you obtain:

Deviance Information Criterion (DIC)...............: 12481.61

Deviance Information Criterion (DIC, saturated) ....: 4186.50

Effective number of parameters .....................: -758.54


Watanabe-Akaike information criterion (WAIC) ...: 14445.87

Effective number of parameters.................: 667.39


Marginal log-Likelihood: -7648.46


I would really appreciate any explanation about these differences.


Thanks in advance to everyone and best regards.

Javier

messages.author: 3eab71733027a24a
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Questions About Large Differences Between DIC and WAIC
parts:
DIC and WAIC are different and does not always agree, although they usually do.

WAIC has a better (Bayesian) justification and is to be preferred

if the results are very sensitive, it can be some issues with data, or rather a
data/model conflict


with DIC/WAIC then only relative numbers makes sense, so comparing absolute
numbers is less meaningful.

You might chose to use CPO instead, or better, the group-version of it, see
vignette in the R-INLA package.
